title: Neuromorphic engineering
text:
13_04  NEUROMORPHIC ENGINEERING

This is the section closest to a mechatronics degree. Neuromorphic engineering builds hardware, chips and sensors, whose design borrows principles from nervous systems: spikes as events, computation in memory, massive parallelism, analogue physics as computation, and local learning. Its motivation is partly scientific (building brains to understand them) and largely practical: the brain performs perception and control on roughly 20 watts, while training and running large AI models consumes megawatts in data centres. Understanding why that gap exists, and how much of it neuromorphic designs can close, requires both the neuroscience in this book and some computer architecture.

WHY CONVENTIONAL COMPUTERS ARE INEFFICIENT FOR NEURAL NETWORKS

A conventional computer follows the von Neumann architecture: a processor and a separate memory connected by a bus. To compute y = W x for a large layer, the processor must fetch each weight from memory. In modern chips, moving data from off-chip DRAM costs far more energy than the arithmetic performed on it; Mark Horowitz's widely cited 2014 estimates for a 45 nm process put a 32-bit DRAM access at hundreds of times the energy of a 32-bit floating-point addition. Deep learning is dominated by such data movement, the "memory wall".

The brain has no separation between memory and processor. A synapse stores its weight and applies it, at the same place. Communication is sparse: a typical cortical neuron fires at a few spikes per second on average, and only when it has something to signal. Computation is asynchronous, without a global clock. Neuromorphic engineering tries to copy these three features: co-located memory and compute, sparse event-driven communication, and asynchrony.

CARVER MEAD AND ANALOGUE VLSI

The field was founded by Carver Mead at Caltech in the late 1980s. Mead, a pioneer of VLSI chip design, noticed that a MOS transistor operated in the subthreshold regime, where the gate voltage is below the threshold, conducts a current that depends exponentially on gate voltage:

  I_ds approximately I_0 exp( kappa V_gs / U_T )

where U_T = kT/q is the thermal voltage, about 25 mV at room temperature, and kappa is a coupling factor less than 1. This is the same Boltzmann physics that governs ion channels: the open probability of a voltage-gated channel also depends exponentially on voltage over the relevant range, because both involve charges crossing an energy barrier (compare the Boltzmann factors in the Nernst equation, Chapter 2). Mead argued that physics itself could compute: currents add by Kirchhoff's law, capacitors integrate, and exponential transistors multiply and divide via logarithms. Rather than represent numbers as bits and simulate equations, one could build circuits whose physics obeys the equations directly, with tiny currents and therefore tiny power.

His 1989 book "Analog VLSI and Neural Systems" and his 1990 paper "Neuromorphic electronic systems" in the Proceedings of the IEEE established the field and the name. With his student Misha Mahowald he built a silicon retina, with photoreceptors, horizontal-cell-like resistive networks computing local averages, and outputs signalling differences from that average, an analogue implementation of the centre-surround processing described in Chapter 8. Mahowald also developed the address-event representation (AER), a protocol for communicating spikes between chips: when a neuron spikes, its address is sent on a shared digital bus, and the receiver reconstructs which neuron fired. AER remains the standard way to communicate spikes in neuromorphic systems.

Analogue circuits have a weakness: transistors vary from one to another (device mismatch), drift with temperature, and are noisy. The brain tolerates variability too, and some researchers argue neuromorphic systems should learn to tolerate it. But mismatch makes reproducible programming difficult, which is one reason many later systems are digital.

EVENT CAMERAS

The most commercially successful neuromorphic device so far is the event camera, or dynamic vision sensor (DVS). Each pixel independently and asynchronously outputs an event when the logarithm of its light intensity changes by more than a threshold:

  event (x, y, t, polarity) when | log I(x,y,t) - log I(x,y,t_last) | > C

There are no frames. A static scene produces almost no data; a moving edge produces a stream of events with microsecond timing. Patrick Lichtsteiner, Christoph Posch and Tobi Delbruck described an influential 128 by 128 pixel version in 2008. The log-intensity response gives wide dynamic range, analogous to adaptation in photoreceptors, and the change detection resembles transient retinal ganglion cells. Event cameras are attractive for high-speed robotics, drones, and automotive sensing because of low latency, low power and resilience to motion blur and extreme lighting. Their output does not suit standard frame-based CNNs directly, so researchers use spiking networks, convert events into frame-like tensors, or design event-native networks; Guillermo Gallego and colleagues reviewed the field in 2019 (later published in IEEE TPAMI). Silicon cochleas, which output events for frequency channels, were developed on similar principles.

LARGE DIGITAL NEUROMORPHIC CHIPS

Several large systems took a digital, event-driven approach:

SpiNNaker, led by Steve Furber at the University of Manchester (Furber was one of the designers of the original ARM processor), connects very many small ARM cores with a packet-switched network optimised for delivering tiny spike packets to many destinations. Its largest machine, completed around 2018, has about one million cores and was designed for real-time simulation of large spiking networks for neuroscience, within the Human Brain Project. A second generation, SpiNNaker2, developed with TU Dresden, added accelerators for machine learning operations.

TrueNorth, from IBM Research and described by Paul Merolla, Dharmendra Modha and colleagues in Science in 2014, integrated one million digital spiking neurons and 256 million synapses on a single chip with 4,096 cores, consuming around 70 milliwatts while running a real-time object detection network. Each core combined memory for synaptic connections with neuron circuits, directly addressing the memory wall. Training networks for it required constraining them to its low-precision, binary-spike format.

Loihi, from Intel and described by Mike Davies and colleagues in IEEE Micro in 2018, added programmable on-chip learning rules, including spike-timing-dependent and three-factor rules (Chapter 7), so the chip could learn locally without an external computer. Loihi 2 followed in 2021, and Intel announced a large system named Hala Point in 2024, built from many Loihi 2 chips.

BrainScaleS, from Heidelberg University, uses analogue neuron circuits running much faster than biological real time, so that long learning experiments can be compressed.

Other designs and startups target low-power edge applications such as keyword spotting, gesture recognition and anomaly detection, where always-on sensing on a milliwatt budget matters.

IN-MEMORY COMPUTING AND MEMRISTORS

A different route to co-locating memory and computation uses resistive devices in crossbar arrays. Put conductances G_ij at the crosspoints of horizontal and vertical wires. Apply voltages V_j to the columns; by Ohm's law each device passes current G_ij V_j, and by Kirchhoff's current law each row wire sums them:

  I_i = sum over j of G_ij V_j

That is a matrix-vector multiplication, the core operation of neural networks, done in one analogue step where the weights are stored. Leon Chua proposed the memristor in 1971 as a theoretical fourth circuit element whose resistance depends on the history of current through it. In 2008 Dmitri Strukov, Stanley Williams and colleagues at HP Labs reported in Nature a titanium dioxide device they identified with memristive behaviour. Phase-change memory, resistive RAM, ferroelectric devices and flash cells have all been explored as analogue synaptic weights, by IBM and many academic groups. The appeal is a synapse that both stores a weight and multiplies by it, and whose conductance can be changed by voltage pulses in a way loosely like LTP and LTD. The challenges are familiar to any hardware engineer: limited precision, noise, drift over time, nonlinear and asymmetric updates, device-to-device variation, and the cost of analogue-to-digital converters at the periphery.

HOW MUCH ENERGY DO SPIKES REALLY SAVE?

Honest comparison is subtle. A spiking network saves energy when activity is sparse, because operations happen only when spikes arrive, and an accumulate (adding a weight when a binary spike arrives) is cheaper than a multiply-accumulate. But if a spiking network needs many timesteps to represent a value with spike counts, the savings can disappear. Meanwhile, conventional accelerators such as GPUs and TPUs have become far more efficient through low-precision arithmetic and sparsity of their own. Benchmarks published by neuromorphic researchers have shown advantages for certain workloads, such as some sparse, temporal and latency-sensitive tasks, while dense, large-batch deep learning remains dominated by conventional accelerators. The field's own community has noted the need for fair, standardised benchmarks; the NeuroBench effort, organised by many groups, aims to provide them.

It is also worth estimating the brain's efficiency. With about 86 billion neurons, around 20 watts total, and average firing rates of perhaps a few hertz, the brain's energy per synaptic event is very low, though estimates vary widely depending on assumptions. Peter Lennie in 2003 estimated from energy budgets that only a small fraction of cortical neurons can be highly active at any time, a constraint that strongly favours sparse codes (13_01).

CONNECTIONS TO AI AND MACHINE LEARNING

1. Algorithms and hardware co-evolve. Deep learning succeeded partly because its operations, dense matrix multiplications, map perfectly onto GPUs. Sara Hooker called this the "hardware lottery": research ideas succeed in part because they suit available hardware. Spiking networks lost that lottery on GPUs; neuromorphic hardware is an attempt to provide a different ticket.

2. Training spiking networks. Surrogate gradients (13_02) and conversion of trained conventional networks into spiking ones made spiking networks competitive on some benchmarks. Converting ReLU networks works because a spiking neuron's firing rate approximates a rectified linear function of input (the f-I curve of 13_02).

3. On-chip learning and continual learning. Local learning rules on chips such as Loihi aim to let devices adapt after deployment, connecting to the continual learning problem of Chapter 11. Hebbian and three-factor rules suit hardware because they need only locally available signals.

4. Sparsity and conditional computation. Mainstream AI is moving toward brain-like sparsity: mixture-of-experts models activate only some parameters per token, activation sparsity and pruning reduce computation, and low-bit quantisation shrinks memory traffic. These are the same principles neuromorphic engineering began with, arrived at from the direction of scaling.

5. Analogue AI accelerators. In-memory computing with resistive crossbars is now pursued as an accelerator for conventional neural network inference, not only spiking ones, showing that neuromorphic ideas can influence AI hardware even when the network is not brain-like.

6. Robotics. For a mechatronics student, event cameras plus spiking or recurrent controllers on low-power chips are a realistic path to fast, efficient closed-loop control, for example in high-speed drones, where latency matters more than raw accuracy.

SUMMARY

Neuromorphic engineering, founded by Carver Mead on the shared Boltzmann physics of transistors and ion channels, builds sensors and processors that compute with events, in memory, and in parallel. Event cameras are its clearest commercial success; large chips such as SpiNNaker, TrueNorth and Loihi showed scalable spiking hardware; memristive crossbars compute matrix products by Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws. Whether these designs beat conventional accelerators depends on workload and sparsity, but the principles they champion are increasingly shaping mainstream AI hardware.
